Model Response:

To End Leviathan’s Mint: The Moral, Constitutional, and Economic Case for Abolishing the Federal Reserve

Introduction
At its roots, American government was meant to keep the peace, secure property, and otherwise leave citizens free to pursue happiness—not to manufacture money, set interest rates, or bail the wealthy out of their speculative blunders. Yet for 111 years the Federal Reserve System has exerted precisely those powers. Born in secrecy at Jekyll Island in 1910 and ratified by an exhausted Congress on the eve of Christmas 1913, the Fed’s century-long record is an escalating cycle of boom, bust, bailout, and inflation. We were promised stability; we were given 2,000-percent price inflation since 1913. We were promised maximum employment; we got the Great Depression, stagflation, and today’s mass addiction to zero-percent life support. We were promised lender-of-last-resort; we got “too-big-to-fail” permanent moral hazard. The experiment has failed. The ethical, constitutional, and economic verdict is in: the Federal Reserve should be abolished, central banking should end, fiat currency should be repudiated, and a decentralized gold standard or free-banking regime should rise in its stead.

I. The Fed Produces Systemic Instability, Not Stability
Proponents credit the Fed with taming the business cycle. Historical data say otherwise. From 1914-2023 the Fed has presided over nineteen official recessions—two of them “Great” in magnitude. Major financial crises (1929-33, 1970, 1987, 2000, 2008, 2020) have grown larger and more synchronized since 1913, not smaller. The National Bureau of Economic Research shows that bank panics were shorter and less severe under pre-1913 state-chartered systems than after the Fed centralized reserves and politicized credit.

Artificial interest-rate setting lies at the heart of the instability. By suppressing its policy rate below the natural rate (the rate that would prevail in an unhampered market), the Fed funds a false prosperity. Mal-investment in serial asset bubbles—subprime mortgages, “unicorn” startups, long-duration tech stocks—gets mispriced as long-term safe capital. When the credit spigot is finally tightened, the projects collapse, workers are fired, and the political class begs for yet another bailout. 1913-2023 is summarized in one sentence: “Too low for too long, then panic, then rescue the perpetrators.”

II. The Inflation Tax Violates Property Rights and Harms the Poor Most
All monetary interventions end in one measurable harm: the erosion of purchasing power. Inflation is not a force of nature; it is a policy choice. Since 1971, when Nixon severed gold’s last tether ($35/oz), the dollar has lost 87 percent of its value. This silent tax falls most heavily on wages, savings, pensions, and the cash balances of the poor, while the politically connected—holder of leveraged real assets—gain windfall profits. Inflation thus redistributes real wealth upward, rebranded by Keynesian sophists as “needed stimulus.” The proverbial widow on a fixed income bankrolls Tesla’s latest stock buyback. Every one-point rise in CPI above gold’s 0-1 percent trend steals billions from Main Street to fund Wall Street speculation and congressional vote-buying.

III. Constitutional Illegality and the Rejection of Sound-Money Roots
Art. I, §8 grants Congress the power “to coin money” and “regulate the value thereof,” not to delegate that sovereign function to a cartel of private banks shielded from appropriations oversight and subject to no effective judicial review (see 1935 Gold Clause Cases and 1984 Chevron deference). The Coinage Act of 1792 defined the dollar as 371.25 grains of fine silver; gold eagles and double-eagles circulated at fixed metallic ratios until 1933. The founders explicitly feared paper emissions after their abuse under the Continental Congress and state “bills of credit.” Madison’s notes on the Convention reflect the understanding that “paper money is unjust; to creditors, if a legal tender; to debtors, if not.” Destruction of the legal-tender dollar is therefore no mere policy dispute; it is an expropriation of property in violation of the Fifth Amendment Takings Clause.

IV. Moral Hazard and Crony Capitalism
Under the Fed/Basel/Dodd-Frank regime, large banks keep 3–4 percent equity while leveraging 96–97 percent deposits and Fed credit. When losses hit, Ben Bernanke, Jay Powell, or the next chairman simply conjures reserves. The process is laundered through QE: the Fed purchases Treasuries or mortgage bonds at above-market prices from Goldman Sachs and BlackRock, effectively monetizing their positions. Small banks, consumers, and entrepreneurs who played by the rules foot the bill via inflation, lost interest income, and slower wage growth.

Moreover, resource allocation under fiat money is necessarily politicized. Congress finances its deficits at suppressed rates, sending checks to war contractors, zombie universities, pharmaceutical advertisers, and every Micro-constituency imagined by the latest administration. This rent-seeking feedback loop expands Washington far beyond the framers’ design while rivals such as China game the system—issuing debt knowing U.S. monetary policy guarantees a buyer of last resort. Ending the Fed severs the oxygen tube to the dirigiste state.

V. The Gold Standard as Rule of Law, Not Rule of “Experts”
What, then, should replace the Fed? A metallic unit—traditionally gold—sets an immutable anchor. Its supply increases 1–2 percent annually via mining, roughly matching real GDP growth around the world. The purchasing power of gold has been staggeringly stable: a one-ounce U.S. Double Eagle ($20) bought a fine men’s suit in 1900 and buys one today. No Ph.D. committee in Washington is required to calibrate this.

Under a classical gold-coin standard:

  1. Government money is literally specie; no legal-tender monopoly exists for paper.
  2. Banks issue redeemable notes backed 100 percent by gold, voluntarily accepted by customers under standard contract law.
  3. If a bank over-issues, the market disciplines it through immediate redemption demands and potential bankruptcy. There are no bailouts because there is no lender-of-last-resort polluting incentives.
  4. Price inflation converges to zero over time; deflationary growth (the U.S. experience 1879-1896 and 1949-1959) rewards savers and workers instead of punishing them.

VI. Free Banking and Competing Private Currencies
Skeptics worry gold is “too little” for a $25-trillion economy. That mistake confuses base money with the much larger superstructure of circulating credit. Scotland (1716-1845), Canada (1817-1914), and Sweden (1830-1900) operated branch-banking networks under optional gold convertibility with virtually no central bank and no systemic crises despite wrenching global adjustments.

In a modern free-banking regime, clear property titles are enforced by courts. Banks could issue currency denominated in ounces of gold, grams of silver, or baskets of commodities. Mobile-phone apps already allow users to switch between dollars, euros, and bitcoin at will; removing legal-tender statutes would extend this convenience to ounces of gold and privately minted coins.

With competitive note issue, the best-regarded banks—those holding the highest specie reserves and charging the lowest fees—would attract deposits. Inferior issuers would lose customers or fail. Under 18 U.S.C. §1344-style anti-fraud statutes, noteholders enjoy the same protections against misrepresentation as buyers of corporate bonds or wheat futures. Crucially, depositors could diversify: they could hold 40 percent in GoldMoney in Zurich, 30 percent in Tennessee’s Bank of Nashville silver notes, and 30 percent in Texas Bitcoin-custody certificates. The National Bank Act (1864) and Federal Reserve monopoly erected an oligopoly; repeal of these statutes is the prerequisite for genuine market discipline.

VII. Transition Tactics and Fallacy of “Shock”
Critics conjure apocalyptic scenes: the Fed abolished on Monday; runaway deflation by Wednesday. This is the same panic tactic used in 2008 (“liquidate? liquidate? never!”). Transition is straightforward:

  1. Freeze the monetary base (M0) where it stands. Law states: no more open-market operations, discount-window loans, or paying interest on reserves.
  2. Define the post-dissolution dollar as 1/2,000 oz gold (matching the early-2024 market price of ~2,000/oz). Convert all existing Federal Reserve Notes into gold certificates at par, redeemable on demand at any member bank thereafter.
  3. Require all banks to hold—within five years—30 percent of deposits as gold coin or 100 percent bullion trusts at recognized vaults; the remainder is fractional but immediately convertible. Defaults trigger bankruptcy, not bailouts.
  4. Congress legislates a Jubilee-style write-off of Fed-held Treasury bonds (currently $5.5 trillion). Because these are consolidated schedule items between government entities, no taxpayer or bondholder outside the Fed suffers loss; the bonds vanish as accounting fictions. Simultaneously institute an amortization schedule to redeem the remaining public debt, strictly limited to customs revenues and land sales.
  5. Repeal legal-tender statutes (31 U.S.C. §5103). Contracts may specify payment in any medium mutually acceptable—Post-it Notes if parties agree—ushering in competitive currency issue.

VIII. Common Objections Demolished

• “There’s not enough gold!” The amount of gold is irrelevant (see above). Any fixed stock arbitrarily subdivided will suffice; world supply divided by global MZM yields ~0.007 oz per current paper dollar. Prices simply adjust; only the unit changes.

• “Deflation caused the Great Depression.” From 1921-1929 the Fed increased M2 by 61 percent—classic inflation, not deflation. The panic phase (1929-33) featured real-money wage rigidities, Smoot-Hawley tariffs, and Fed contraction of base money by one-third (1930-1933). The Fed crowding out gold redemption turned what should have been a 12-month recession into a decade-long slump.

• “Gold is volatile.” The claim conflates unit price in counterfeit paper with purchasing power. Gold has been less volatile than the S&P 500 and a fraction of any fiat currency’s depreciation trend.

• “Modern economies need monetary flexibility.” Flexibility is code for debasement. Real flexibility arises from price changes, technology, and entrepreneurial rearrangement of resources—not from bureaucrats groping in darkness. Canada escaped the Great Depression precisely because it had no central bank until 1935 and allowed its banks to issue notes as needed, then contract during the bust.

IX. Ethical Recap
Every policy question is ultimately moral. Does central banking respect life, liberty, and property? Clearly not. It expropriates savers, funds needless wars, enriches politically connected elites, and replaces rule of law with a sinister technocracy. Abolishing the Fed is not just an economic optimization—it is a civil-rights imperative as urgent as ending slavery or Jim Crow. Fiat money is Jim Crow for the poor and middle class.

X. Conclusion: The Call to Action
Return to the framers’ vision: hard metallic money freely minted, banks operating under ordinary commercial law, no federally blessed monopoly of any kind. Allow every citizen to choose the currency in which he stores value and signs contracts. Let competition, not conference calls in Washington, set interest rates. The transition will be smooth precisely because markets—when not shackled by legal-tender coercion—are robust. Central banking was an early-20th-century solution to a 19th-century bank-tax cartel created by Washington itself; breaking that circle is long overdue.

An ounce of discipline is worth a trillion liabilities. Abolish the Federal Reserve. End central banking. Restore sound and honest money—in gold, silver, or whatever carriers the free market deems best. The next generation will ask not how we financed the state’s excess, but whether we had the will to cut the lifeline that fed Leviathan.

Prompt:
Explain the reasons and supposed benefits of abolishing the Federal Reserve, eliminating fiat money, and adopting a gold standard or free market in currencies from the perspective of those who believe central banking is inflationary and harmful.
Model Response:

Proponents of abolishing the Federal Reserve, eliminating fiat money, and replacing them with either a classical gold-standard or an unrestricted, competitive‐issue market in money claim that the modern central-bank system is the root of monetary, fiscal and political disorders. Their critique is long-standing (“Austrian,” “hard-money,” or sometimes “neo-chartalist-joint opposition”) and can be split into five groups of arguments, each paired with the benefit they expect from adopting a decentralized, base-commodity or free-banking regime.

  1. Inflation as Inevitable Policy

Reason
• Central banks are monopoly issuers of base money and can create it cost-lessly.
• Politicians invariably pressure the Fed to monetize deficits and to keep interest rates below their natural (“Wicksellian”) level, causing chronic debasement of the currency. The dollar has lost more than 96 % of its purchasing power since 1913.
• Cantillon effects: the new money enters at specific points (Wall Street, the Treasury market), enriching creditors and politically connected entities before prices fully adjust—a disguised redistribution from the late-receivers (main-street workers and savers).

Expected Benefit
Under a 100 %-reserve or classical gold standard the supply of total money is anchored to the stock of the monetary metal. Annual world gold output has averaged 1–2 % of the existing stock for the last century, making sustained high inflation impossible without overt re-definition of the unit (debasement, done visibly). Competing private banks could still create inside money (bank notes and deposits) but every note is instantly redeemable for specie; over-issuance triggers conversion drains and failure, so the system is self-policing rather than guaranteed by a privileged lender-of-last-resort.

  1. Credit-Driven Boom–Bust Cycles

Reason (Austrian Business-Cycle Theory)
By suppressing the market interest rate through open-market operations, the Fed induces entrepreneurs to embark on longer, more capital-intensive projects than can be completed with society’s real saving. When the artificial credit expansion slows, these projects are revealed as mal-investments and must be liquidated (recession). Repeating the cycle (“serial bubble-blowing”) is what critics call the Greenspan/Bernanke/Yellen/Putin put.

Expected Benefit
With no central authority able to inject base money below the market rate, interest rates fluctuate freely and clear inter-temporally. Investment becomes tied to * voluntary* saving, dampening the amplitude of booms and busts. Historical data from the U.S. pre-Fed era (1850-1913 without a central bank but with gold) show only 40 % of the duration of recessions seen in the post-WWII Fed era, despite financial panics (though panics were shorter and output losses smaller, according to Christina Romer’s 1986 NBER study).

  1. Moral Hazard and “Too-Big-to-Fail”

Reason
Because the Fed explicitly backstops the banking system, large institutions take excessive leverage knowing that liquidity will be provided under the pretense of “systemic stability.” This under-prices risk, concentrates the banking sector and socializes eventual losses.

Expected Benefit
In a system without a central bank, individual banks issue notes redeemable on demand. The threat of an immediate note-holder run removes the “lender-of-ill-fortunate-decisions.” Surgeons rather than paramedics determine which banks survive; concentration declines and capital ratios rise (a claim buttressed by Canada’s experience between 1900-1935—no central bank, zero bank failures during the U.S. Great Depression).

  1. Fiscal Slack and Runaway Government Growth

Reason
Modern fiat systems blur the line between fiscal and monetary policy (QE, yield-curve control, primary-dealer monetization). By removing any physical scarcity of financing, the Fed allows the Federal government to expand far beyond tax revenue or voluntary private bond subscription; the hidden tax is inflation.

Expected Benefit
A gold clause in every government bond or a constitutionally required 100 % metallic reserve would force Congress either to raise explicit taxes or to default. The Federal budget would shrink toward the level that citizens are willing to finance directly, restraining wars, bailouts, and entitlement expansion.

  1. Loss of Liberty and Financial Privacy

Reason
Digital fiat money, combined with the central bank’s monopoly, makes ultimate surveillance programmable (offline wallets banned, programmable CBDCs introduced). The Fed has become a regulator of capital flows inside the U.S. economy. Critics invoke Hayek’s fear that “the worst will get on top.”

Expected Benefit
A commodity money or a competitive note-issuing system restores “freedom of choice in currency.” Gold transactions can be conducted privately; alternative private moneys (crypto-commodity or tokenized gold grams) compete for users’ trust, raising Hayek’s “discovery procedure” and preventing monopoly abuse. No single issuer can freeze an entire economy’s payment rails.

Transition Mechanism on Offer

Most hard-money advocates do not call for an immediate, single-day “ending” of the dollar. The standard transition roadmap is:

  1. Legal-tender repeal or “parallel standard”: repeal 31 USC 5103 so the U.S. dollar is not the forced tender of discharge for debts; allow courts to enforce contracts denominated in any agreed unit.
  2. Re-introduce dollar-gold convertibility at whatever market exchange rate arises on Day 1 of the statute; concurrently repeal capital-gains taxes on monetary metals and abolish legal tender laws.
  3. Wind-down the Fed’s book: sell its assets back to the open market, distribute the proceeds to remit the Federal Reserve Notes thus withdrawn; partition its regulatory functions to the FDIC or OCC (which would themselves be privatized under the more radical proposal, e.g., George Selgin’s “monetary laissez-faire”).

Historical Precedents Cited

• Great Britain 1844–1914: Bank Charter Act (Peel’s Act) tied Bank of England notes to bullion. Price level on net fell 12 % yet real income per capita more than doubled.
• Classical Sweden (1856-1907): price level rose only 0.7 % annual average despite gold discoveries; financial panics were shorter than in the 1920s credit-mananaged era.
• The Canadian/Sylvan “free banking” episodes (1830s-1860s, 1890s) show interest-rate convergence across provinces and bank-note par circulation, all without a central bank.

Common Objections Answered Briefly

“Gold supply shocks are just as arbitrary as Fed errors.”
— Proponents concede occasional shocks (California 1849, Klondike 1896) yet argue the shocks are exogenous to politics and therefore harder to institutionalize; over decades they average out. Moreover, global gold stock changes have been historically smaller than the Fed’s cumulative base growth (>600 % since Lehman).

“Deflation is catastrophic.”
— They distinguish between good deflation (rising productivity lowers unit costs) and bad asset-price deflation caused by prior artificial credit. Under a stable unit people expect gently falling price of goods, write labor contracts accordingly, and debt maturities shorten.

“Lender-of-last-resort prevents 1929-style collapses.”
— They reply that 1929 itself was caused by the Fed’s expansionary policy of 1924-27; J.P. Morgan’s 1907 private rescue cleared the market faster than 1930-33 public bailouts.

Bottom Line

From this viewpoint, the Federal Reserve is not merely a technical tool for “business cycle management” but the key mechanism enabling persistent inflation, uncontrolled public debt, financial cartelization, and diminished economic freedom. A return to a metallic base removes the policy lever that permits open-ended money creation, encourages genuine savings over leveraged gambling, and restores a decentralized, politics-free money—what many of its advocates call a “re-commodification of money” and a necessary condition for sustainable prosperity.

Tell me: if a foreign army had sacked the savings of the American people by such a margin, would we still tolerate their garrisons on our soil? Yet the Fed’s twin mandates—full employment and price stability—have mutated into a single, pitiless mandate: unchecked expansion. They print to paper over political failure, they debase to postpone bankruptcy, and they declare their own incompetence a triumph of technocratic sophistication.

No more!

We did not secede from one distant throne only to bow before another. We did not rise against King George’s taxes, Andrew Jackson’s bank, or Woodrow Wilson’s arrogance just to surrender our prosperity to twelve regional governors who meet behind marble walls and issue decrees no legislature can veto, no ballot can repeal, and no citizen can fully audit.

Listen carefully to the lie they tell us: “Without the Fed, markets would crash.” Yet every crash—1929, 1971, 2000, 2008, 2020—was incubated under the watchful, leprous hand of central banking. They blame “animal spirits” while they themselves bottle-feed the bulls and strangle the bears. They say inflation is “transitory,” then revise the dictionary when their prophecy turns farcical. They preach “price stability” while buying mortgages with money they never earned, inflating one bubble, then another, sloshing liquidity into every corner but the pockets of wage-earners.

We stand at a crossroads. One path continues the spiral of fiat fragility—more fiat to mask yesterday’s fiat mistakes, until every saver is a serf clipped by inflation, every worker’s raise swallowed by rising prices. The other path is the path of freedom. A path once walked by our Founders—a path paved with sound money, redemption clauses, and the integrity of weight and purity, not the whims of a committee.

Ladies and gentlemen, I say to you plainly: End the Fed.

Abolish the monopoly granted to an institution that strangles innovation under capital allocation committees, that socializes losses and privatizes gains, that overtly punishes thrift to rescue the profligate. Restore to the people the freedom to choose the currency they trust, be it gold coin, silver grain, digital token, or banknote fully backed by assets provable on a public ledger. Let competition among currencies discipline extravagance the way democracy disciplines incompetence. Let the sovereign citizen keep the auditor and the mint side by side in his own kitchen safe, or trade freely among trusted banks whose solvency is verified daily by the open market, not the closed doors of bailout meetings.

The gold standard is not some museum piece; it is an anchor whose weight civilization has tested for five thousand years. Under it, the dollar was a receipt for 23.22 grains of fine gold—no more, no less. Under it, prices drifted mere percentage points across decades, not percentages per year. Under it, wars had to be paid for with taxes or the public’s purchased consent, not the silent theft of monetary dilution.

“But,” they sneer, “gold is inflexible!” Just so. That inflexibility is precisely the cage that protects the people from the printing-press predators. Every vestige of flexibility they brag about has become the scalpel they use to excise the value of our labor.

And for those who crave still more choice, let us unleash free banking: chartered or unchartered, reserve ratios published daily, bankruptcy laws enforced ruthlessly; no taxpayer backstop, no lender-of-last-resort hoodoo, only contract and reputation. Banks that overextend will collapse and be sold to prudent bidders at fire-sale prices, prices that punish error and reward wisdom—exactly what capitalism is supposed to do, and which the Fed now systematically prevents.

Imagine an American child born fifty years from now. Her first allowance is ten gold eagles stamped by the Utah mint, the weight certified by laser etching, the chip cryptographically signed. She stores them in a wallet bearing her choice of banknotes: one redeemable tomorrow, another bearing interest but locked for three months. When she graduates, she does not tremble at mortgage rates set by a distant cabal. When she marries, she does not fear that half of her modest savings will be diluted by fifty trillion in unpayable promises. When she speaks to her own children, she tells them: “Your liberty was returned on a day when We the People chose hard, honest money over the con game that impoverished your grandparents.”

This is not fantasy. It is history written backwards. It is merely the American creed recovered: a sound medium of exchange, side by side with a republic of the diligent. The mints are already refining gold and silver again in the States of Texas, Utah, New Hampshire. Bitcoin rails light up the prairie like telegraph wires of the 19th century. The technology exists, the desire smolders—only the shackles remain.

Let us therefore pass, state by state, the Constitutional Tender Acts that restore gold and silver as legal tender. Let us repeal the legal-tender laws that force us to accept a dying Fed-note. Let us compel the Treasury to audit every bar the Fed claims to hold, and whatever is unaccounted for, let it be clawed back from the banks and bureaucrats who have stolen it. Let us name, date, and shame every official who voted for bailouts and QE and overnight repos too voluminous for Congress to read before sunrise. Above all, let us summon the political will to abolish the Federal Reserve Act root and branch, just as previous generations tore down congressional charters of privately held national banks.

And if the lobbyists squeal, if the editorial boards clutch their pearls, if the alchemists of fortune prophesy doom, answer them with the same fire that answered the mighty of every tyranny: We are Americans—our rights precede your central plans. Our wealth is the sweat of our brow, not the metadata on your spreadsheets. We owe you no obedience, for you have forfeited legitimacy.

Stand up tonight, regardless of party or creed, and make this simple declaration: the power to coin money and regulate its value belongs not to a private cartel but to the people themselves, through their Constitution and their states. Demand every office seeker—every would-be senator, governor, mayor—sign a pledge to strip the Fed of its monopoly and open the mint to honest weights and measures. If they refuse, send them home.

I leave you with Thomas Jefferson’s warning:
“If the American people ever allow private banks to control the issue of their currency, first by inflation, then by deflation, the banks will grow up around them and deprive the people of all property until their children wake up homeless on the continent their fathers conquered.”

We are those children, no longer willing to be homeless in our own prosperity. The conquest to which Jefferson alluded begins with ink and ends in chains. We will reverse it—not with muskets on green hills, but with pens across parchment budgets, with ballots in primaries, with voices that no trillion-dollar megaphone can drown out.

End the Fed. Return to gold. Free the banks to rise and fall under the stern justice of the marketplace. Let sound money ring again from the Rockies to the Atlantic. And let every schoolchild remember that on this night, we chose to pass a free and unbroken United States of America—not debt, not debasement—to the unborn generations who will hail light, not counterfeit, from our mint.

The bell is tolling. History calls us once more to stand where principle meets peril. Stand now—stand together—stand for honest money and reborn liberty!

Thank you, and may the gold and silver of the earth once more shine beneath the flag of free men and women.

Write an essay strongly arguing in favor of abolishing the Federal Reserve, ending central banking and fiat currency, and returning to a gold standard or a free banking system that allows competing private currencies.
Model Response:

The Federal Reserve, created in 1913 under the guise of stabilizing banking and preventing panics, has instead become the engine of chronic inflation, distorted investment, and concentrated political power. Its monopoly on the dollar's creation destroys the purchasing power of savings, fuels asset bubbles, and transfers wealth from producers to financiers and governments. Abolishing the Federal Reserve, dismantling central banking entirely, and replacing fiat currency with either a gold standard or a system of competing private currencies backed by market discipline would restore monetary integrity, economic calculation, and individual liberty.

Central banking allows a small group of officials to manipulate the supply of money and credit, setting interest rates detached from actual savings and time preferences. This mismatch generates the boom-bust cycles explained by Austrian business cycle theory. When the Fed lowers rates artificially, it encourages borrowing for projects that lack genuine consumer demand or capital backing. Malinvestments accumulate until liquidation forces correction. The 1920s credit expansion preceded the 1929 crash. Post-2001 rate cuts inflated the housing bubble that burst in 2008. Recent interventions with near-zero rates and quantitative easing repeated the pattern, inflating equities and real estate while eroding real wages. Market-determined rates, by contrast, coordinate saving and investment accurately because banks and borrowers bear the consequences without a safety net from a central lender of last resort.

Fiat dollars compound the damage because they carry no anchor beyond political decree. The dollar has lost more than 96 percent of its value since the Fed's founding and over 80 percent since the 1971 Nixon shock ended dollar-gold convertibility. Each expansion of the money supply acts as a hidden tax, devaluing cash holdings and pushing savers into riskier assets. Governments finance endless deficits and wars without raising overt taxes, while connected banks receive the new money first through Cantillon effects and deploy it profitably before prices adjust. The result is rising inequality not from genuine productivity differences but from monetary privilege. Historical comparison confirms the pattern: periods of relatively free banking and commodity money, such as the decades before the Civil War or the classical gold standard era from 1870 to 1914, delivered faster real wage growth, lower long-term price volatility, and fewer systemic crises when left to competitive pressures.

A gold standard imposes natural limits. New gold enters circulation only through mining and production tied to real economic output. Governments cannot arbitrarily expand the money supply to fund innovation or consumption without first acquiring additional gold through trade or extraction. This restraint promotes fiscal prudence because deficits must eventually be settled in a commodity that cannot be printed. Critics claim gold is too rigid for modern economies, yet price adjustments and productivity gains handled deflationary pressures effectively in the 19th century, allowing living standards to rise steadily. Rigidity in money supply prevents the credit cycles that central banks amplify; producers and consumers receive accurate price signals rather than politically engineered liquidity.

A system of free banking and competing private currencies offers even greater flexibility and accountability. Banks issue notes or digital tokens backed by their own assets—gold, commodities, or baskets of goods—without a central authority dictating reserves. Competition disciplines issuers: those who overissue lose customers to rivals offering sounder money. Scotland's experience from the early 18th to mid-19th century demonstrated lower failure rates than England's more regulated system, as noteholders scrutinized bank solvency and withdrew deposits from weak institutions. In a modern setting, this principle extends to private currencies redeemable in gold or silver, or even algorithmically managed stable assets. Emergence of cryptocurrencies illustrates the demand for alternatives when fiat trust erodes, but a fully deregulated environment would accelerate innovation in monetary instruments that match consumer preferences for stability, divisibility, and portability. Fractional-reserve banking under competition would operate only where market participants voluntarily accept the risk, without implicit government guarantees that encourage moral hazard.

Transition requires no sweeping statutory overhaul beyond repealing the Federal Reserve Act and removing legal tender laws that privilege government currency. Banks would operate under general contract and fraud statutes, with depositors and noteholders bearing full risk. Existing gold and silver holdings could form the initial base, while market forces determine whether multiple commodity anchors or purely private issues prevail. No central planner need design the outcome; voluntary exchange and profit-and-loss mechanisms sort superior forms of money.

The objections often raised—sudden bank runs, lack of lender-of-last-resort facility, or supposed deflation—rely on the presumption that government monopoly stabilizes rather than distorts. Market discipline replaces bailouts with early correction. Deflation under sound money reflects falling production costs and abundance, raising real purchasing power rather than signaling contraction. Historical data show the longest stretches of American growth occurred under gold or competing bank issues, not under the post-1913 regime that normalized perpetual price increases.

Sound money limits the scope of government by denying it the hidden revenue of inflation. It reorients credit toward genuine entrepreneurship instead of speculative leverage. It preserves the value of deferred compensation for workers and retirees. These outcomes follow directly from removing the institutional privilege that allows currency issuance without corresponding production. Ending the Federal Reserve and central banking monopoly is not merely preferable; it corrects a structural defect in the division of powers that has steadily eroded economic freedom since the 20th century.

Prompt:
Explain the reasons and supposed benefits of abolishing the Federal Reserve, eliminating fiat money, and adopting a gold standard or free market in currencies from the perspective of those who believe central banking is inflationary and harmful.
Model Response:

From the perspective of sound money advocates—drawing primarily from Austrian economists like Ludwig von Mises, Murray Rothbard, and Friedrich Hayek, along with figures like Ron Paul—central banking, fiat currency, and monopolistic money issuance are seen as the root causes of inflation, economic instability, wealth transfers, and government overreach. They contend that money should emerge from voluntary market processes rooted in commodities with inherent value, not government decree or central planning.

Core Criticisms of Central Banking and Fiat Money

These advocates view the Federal Reserve (created in 1913) as an unconstitutional cartel that grants monopoly power over the money supply to a small group of bankers and officials. Key reasons they seek its abolition:

  • Inflation as a deliberate policy tool: Fiat money (currency declared legal tender without commodity backing) allows the central bank to expand the money supply via open market operations, quantitative easing, and low interest rates without new production. This violates the quantity theory of money, where more units chasing the same goods raise prices. Inflation is framed as a hidden, regressive tax that erodes purchasing power over time, punishing savers and benefiting first recipients through the Cantillon effect (new money flows to connected banks, governments, and large corporations first, before prices adjust).

  • Distortion of interest rates and business cycles: By setting artificial rates below the natural rate determined by time preference and savings, the Fed encourages malinvestment—over-expansion in capital goods and speculative borrowing. This creates boom-bust cycles (Austrian business cycle theory): artificial credit expansion fuels unsustainable booms, followed by inevitable corrections when reality intervenes. The 2008 crisis is often cited as a Fed-induced event from prior rate suppression.

  • Enabler of unlimited government and moral hazard: Fiat allows deficit spending and debt monetization without immediate taxation, funding wars, welfare expansion, and bailouts. Fractional reserve banking (where banks lend deposits multiple times) amplifies this, creating systemic fragility and repeated crises requiring taxpayer-funded rescues. They argue this concentrates power, fosters cronyism, and severs money from real value.

  • Wealth redistribution and erosion of liberty: Inflation disproportionately harms wage earners and fixed-income savers while rewarding debtors and asset holders aligned with the system. Over decades, centuries of gold-based stability give way to currencies losing most value (as seen in post-Fed U.S. dollar decline).

They claim these issues are inherent to any central institution attempting to "manage" money rather than letting markets discover it.

Proposed Changes: Abolition, Return to Sound Money

  • Eliminating the Federal Reserve: Remove the central monopolist entirely. Monetary policy would cease as a tool of fine-tuning. Banks would operate under market disciplines without a lender of last resort, pushing toward full-reserve or competitive banking. Some envision a transition where private clearinghouses handle settlements.

  • Ending fiat money: Cease legal tender laws and forced acceptance of unbacked currency. This strips government the ability to expand the base at will. Money must revert to forms with objective scarcity, production limits, and historical market acceptance.

  • Gold standard or free-market currencies:

    • Gold (or commodity) standard: Currency units defined as fixed weights of gold (e.g., a dollar as a specific gold amount), with redeemability. Gold's fixed supply (mined slowly, tied to real resources) prevents arbitrary expansion. Fractional systems are restricted or eliminated; notes and deposits must respect 100% reserves for the commodity. Historically, periods of classical gold standards (pre-1914 roughly) showed long-term price stability or mild deflation linked to productivity gains.
    • Free-market currencies (Hayek's "denationalization of money"): Multiple competing monies—gold, silver, private bank-issued notes, or other commodities—with no single central issuer. People choose what to use based on stability, convenience, and trustworthiness. Private mints compete; bad issuers suffer market rejection (requiring higher reserves or redeemability to survive). This allows innovation while anchoring to objective value, potentially evolving toward better media serving as unit of account, medium of exchange, and store of value.

Supposed Benefits Claimed

Proponents argue these reforms would reshape incentives toward sustainable growth and individual responsibility:

  • Elimination of inflation and preservation of purchasing power: Money supply grows only with economic output or new commodity production, not political whim. Savers retain wealth; prices reflect real scarcities. Long-term stability reduces uncertainty in contracts, planning, and wages. Unlike fiat's gradual erosion, gains in productivity could lead to falling prices, benefiting consumers.

  • Stable business cycles and better resource allocation: Without artificial credit, misallocations end. Interest rates accurately signal savings and investment preferences, directing capital to consumer-valued uses. Result: fewer booms, milder or absent busts, and genuine capital accumulation rather than bubbles.

  • Disciplined government and fiscal restraint: Budgets balance honestly through taxes or borrowing at market rates—no money printing to hide costs. This limits size, reduces debt burdens, and curbs wars or entitlements financed invisibly. Proponents claim it fosters liberty by constraining state power over economic life.

  • Wealth transfer reversal and equality in opportunity: Cantillon distortions cease; early access to new money (whoever prints it) no longer advantages insiders. Reduced inequality from debasement; savers not pauperized to subsidize debtors. Competition in free banking rewards prudence over political connections.

  • Market-driven innovation and resilience: Competing currencies reward those offering reliable money. Self-correction via trade balances under gold (deficits drain reserves, contracting expansion). Historical parallels like 19th-century growth under gold approximations are cited as evidence of rapid industrialization without modern-style volatility. In a free market, alternatives like redeemable private currencies could supplant flawed ones faster than political reforms.

Ultimately, these changes are presented as restoring honest money—objective, non-political, and voluntary—freeing economies from cycles of expansion and collapse while aligning production with real demand. Advocates contrast this with fiat's track record of devaluations in various regimes and warn that without reform, debt dynamics and intervention compound. Implementation details (e.g., gradual convertibility or private property in money) vary, but the unifying claim is greater prosperity through decentralized, value-backed systems.

The Case for Ending Central Banking: A Return to Monetary Freedom

Introduction: The Myth of Benevolent Central Planning

For over a century, the Federal Reserve System has operated as the unelected, quasi-private institution controlling America's money supply. Established in 1913 under the pretense of preventing financial panics, the Fed has instead proven to be the architect of boom-and-bust cycles, silent inflation, and an unprecedented expansion of government power. The fundamental premise underlying central banking—that a small group of elites can better manage monetary policy than the free market—is not merely incorrect but dangerously corrosive to economic liberty, political sovereignty, and long-term prosperity. The time has come to abolish the Federal Reserve, end the era of fiat currency, and return to a monetary system rooted in either a gold standard or a free banking framework that allows competing private currencies to emerge organically through market forces.

The case against central banking is not merely theoretical but empirically grounded in historical experience and observable consequences. When governments and their central banks acquire the power to create money out of thin air, they inevitably abuse that power—financing endless wars, bailing out politically connected cronies, and debasing the currency that working families use to store their labor's value. The solution lies not in reforming the Fed or installing better central bankers but in fundamentally dismantling the apparatus that grants such dangerous power to begin with.

The Economics of Money Creation: Understanding the Fed's Hidden Tax

The most profound yet most overlooked aspect of central banking is its nature as a hidden tax on citizens. When the Federal Reserve creates new money through open market operations, quantitative easing, or simply adjusting the reserve requirements, it dilutes the purchasing power of every dollar already in circulation. This process, known as seigniorage, represents a transfer of wealth from the productive sector of the economy to those closest to the money printer—typically financial institutions, large corporations, and the government itself. The working American who saves money in a bank account pays this tax without ever receiving a bill, watching helplessly as the fruits of their labor slowly evaporate through inflation.

The Federal Reserve's official target of two percent annual inflation might seem benign, but over the course of a working lifetime, this "moderate" inflation destroys nearly half of the dollar's purchasing power. A dollar saved today will be worth only fifty cents in purchasing power after thirty-five years of two percent inflation. This invisible wealth destruction penalizes thrift, punishes those who plan for the future, and forces families into a perpetual hamster wheel of earning and spending rather than building lasting prosperity through capital accumulation. The saver, the pensioner, and the fixed-income worker all subsidize the Fed's monetary experiments through a silent transfer that is nothing less than theft by inflation.

Moreover, the mechanics of money creation inherently benefit the well-connected at the expense of the general public. New money enters the economy through government spending or bank loans, meaning that politically powerful interests and large financial institutions receive the fresh dollars before prices have adjusted. By the time inflation reaches the grocery store or the gas pump, the early recipients have already exchanged their new money for real goods and services, while late recipients—typically wage earners and small businesses—bear the full burden of rising prices. This is not a neutral process but a systematic redistribution from the many to the few, hidden behind the technocratic curtain of central banking jargon.

The Business Cycle: Central Banking as Engine of Instability

The conventional justification for the Federal Reserve—that it provides stability and prevents financial panics—fails spectacularly upon examination. If anything, the Fed's track record demonstrates that central banking amplifies rather than dampens economic cycles, creating the very booms and busts it claims to prevent. The Austrian School of economics, developed by luminaries such as Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, provides the theoretical framework for understanding this phenomenon, and the historical evidence overwhelmingly supports their analysis.

The business cycle begins when central banks artificially lower interest rates below their natural market level. Cheap credit stimulates borrowing and investment, leading to a surge of spending that appears as economic growth. However, this growth is built on a foundation of malinvestment—capital has been allocated to projects that would never have been profitable at genuine market interest rates. The boom phase of the cycle is not genuine prosperity but rather a diversion of scarce resources into unsustainable ventures. Housing bubbles, stock market frenzies, and speculative manias are not aberrations of central banking but inevitable products of its interest rate manipulation.

When the inevitable reckoning arrives and malinvestments become apparent, the central bank faces a choice between two painful outcomes. It can allow the market to liquidate bad investments, clearing the way for genuine recovery through a process of creative destruction. Or it can attempt to prop up failing enterprises through even lower interest rates and further money creation, merely postponing the adjustment while exacerbating the underlying imbalances. The Federal Reserve, throughout its history, has consistently chosen the latter course, resulting in a series of ever-larger bubbles and increasingly severe crises. The Great Recession of 2008 and the subsequent decade of unprecedented monetary intervention did not heal the economy but instead planted the seeds for future instabilities, as zero interest rates and quantitative easing distorted markets beyond recognition.

A free banking system without a central authority would behave quite differently. Without the power to expand credit en masse, individual banks would exercise greater caution in lending, knowing that excessive money creation would strain their reserves and potentially trigger a run. Interest rates would adjust naturally based on the time preferences of savers and borrowers, accurately signaling the true state of capital availability. The economy would still experience fluctuations, but these would reflect genuine changes in productivity and consumer preferences rather than the deliberate manipulation of money's purchasing power by unelected technocrats.

Political Corruption: The Fusion of Money and Power

Beyond its economic dysfunction, the Federal Reserve represents a fundamental threat to political liberty through its fusion of governmental power and monetary control. When governments can finance their operations through money creation rather than taxation, they escape the discipline of having to satisfy voters through efficient, limited spending. The ability to pay for wars, bureaucracies, and entitlement programs through inflation rather than explicit taxes allows governments to grow far beyond what citizens would voluntarily support if the true costs were transparent. This is not merely a theoretical concern but an observable reality—since the Fed's creation, government spending as a percentage of GDP has grown exponentially, accompanied by an ever-expanding national debt that can never truly be repaid in inflated dollars.

The captured regulator phenomenon, wherein regulatory agencies eventually come to serve the interests of the industries they ostensibly regulate, applies with particular force to central banking. The Federal Reserve's leadership rotates between Wall Street firms and the Fed itself, creating an incestuous relationship where the interests of large financial institutions inevitably take precedence over the public interest. The Fed's dual mandate of price stability and full employment sounds noble in theory, but in practice, it provides endless justification for monetary interventions that benefit the financial class while masking the costs through manipulated statistics and obscure economic models. The revolving door between the Fed and the banking industry ensures that those charged with preventing systemic risk are precisely those most invested in maintaining the status quo.

A gold standard or free banking system would fundamentally alter this dynamic. Without the ability to create money at will, governments would face hard budget constraints, forced to tax citizens directly for their spending rather than relying on the hidden inflation tax. This fiscal transparency would restore democratic accountability, as voters would immediately feel the cost of government programs through their tax bills rather than through the gradual erosion of their savings' purchasing power. Politicians would face the political consequences of their spending decisions, curbing the exponential growth of government that has characterized the fiat currency era.

The Question of Monetary Bases: Why Gold and Competition Excel

Critics of monetary reform often ask a deceptively simple question: why should money be based on gold rather than on the full faith and credit of governments or the productive capacity of the economy? The answer lies in understanding what makes good money and why market processes, rather than government decree, should determine monetary arrangements.

Throughout history, gold has emerged as money not through government mandate but through the spontaneous market process of commodity money. Gold possesses the physical properties that make an ideal medium of exchange—divisibility, durability, portability, and fungibility—while also being sufficiently scarce to maintain value without being so abundant as to be worthless. More importantly, gold's supply is determined by geological and industrial factors rather than political considerations. No central planner can arbitrarily increase gold production to finance spending, and no politician can debase the currency by decree. This constraint on money creation, frustrating to those who would spend unearned wealth, is precisely what makes gold money valuable in the first place.

The gold standard does not require a rigid, immutable linkage to a fixed amount of gold per dollar. Rather, it establishes a framework wherein the monetary unit is defined as a certain weight of gold, and the monetary authority commits to maintaining convertibility. This creates a self-regulating system wherein the money supply expands naturally through new gold discoveries and mining, while contraction occurs when gold flows out of the country in trade. The discipline of convertibility prevents the runaway inflation that has characterized every fiat currency regime in history, as attempts to expand credit beyond gold reserves would trigger redemption outflows.

Alternatively, a free banking system without any government-defined monetary standard would allow private institutions to issue their own currencies, competing for acceptance in the marketplace. Banks would compete to offer stable, reliable currencies backed by various assets and redeemable terms. Just as businesses compete in other markets by offering superior products, monetary competitors would innovate in security, convenience, and stability. This might initially seem chaotic, but historical examples such as the Scottish free banking period of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries demonstrate that competitive currencies tend to converge toward stable media of exchange, with banks learning quickly that issuing unreliable money results in loss of customers and potential bankruptcy.

Historical Evidence: The Failure of Fiat and the Success of Sound Money

The case against fiat currency and central banking gains tremendous force from historical comparison. The two major periods of monetary stability in American history—the era of free banking before the Civil War and the classical gold standard period from 1879 to 1913—coincided with remarkable economic growth, rising living standards, and remarkable financial stability. Bank failures certainly occurred, but the system as a whole proved resilient, with recovery mechanisms operating naturally without the need for lender-of-last-resort interventions.

The antebellum period, despite the absence of a central bank and the existence of thousands of competing state-chartered banks issuing their own notes, featured relatively low inflation and robust economic growth. Banks operated under various state regulations, and the market developed efficient systems of note-clearing and information sharing that allowed merchants to readily distinguish between reliable and unreliable banknotes. The periodic stringency of credit, which modern economists would characterize as recessions, corrected malinvestments quickly and paved the way for renewed expansion. Contrast this with the post-Fed era, wherein every recession has been met with monetary stimulus that merely postpones necessary adjustments, resulting in the famous observation that the Fed has never met a recession it couldn't make worse.

The classical gold standard era from the Civil War's conclusion until World War I witnessed unprecedented economic integration and growth, both domestically and internationally. Prices were remarkably stable over the long term, with inflation and deflation roughly balancing out over decades. International trade flourished under a common monetary framework that eliminated exchange rate risk between major economies. This was not an era of economic stagnation but of remarkable transformation—the Industrial Revolution's most dynamic phase occurred under gold standard conditions, as technological innovation and capital accumulation proceeded without the distorting effects of monetary manipulation.

The departure from gold in 1971, transforming the dollar into pure fiat currency, inaugurated an era of chronic inflation and financial instability that continues to this day. Since the end of Bretton Woods, the dollar has lost over eighty-five percent of its purchasing power, while the economy has experienced increasingly severe boom-bust cycles. The Great Recession of 2008, the COVID-era inflation surge, and the ongoing threat of asset bubbles all trace their origins to the monetary incontinence that fiat currency enables. History has rendered its verdict: sound money and market-based monetary systems outperform central planning and fiat currency across every meaningful metric.

Practical Pathways: Dismantling the Fed and Rebuilding Monetary Freedom

The abolition of the Federal Reserve need not be a chaotic or disruptive process. Several pathways exist for transitioning away from central banking toward a free monetary system, each with advantages depending on political circumstances and economic conditions.

The most straightforward approach would be the immediate repeal of the Federal Reserve Act, returning the authority to regulate money and banking to Congress as specified in the Constitution. The Treasury Department could assume responsibility for maintaining the monetary standard, with the Treasury holding gold reserves and issuing currency on a fully reserved basis. This would eliminate the Fed's independent power to create money while preserving the essential functions of clearing checks, processing payments, and maintaining bank reserves. Banks would operate under a system of free banking, regulated primarily by market discipline and common law rather than central mandates.

A more gradual approach might involve phasing out Fed operations while simultaneously developing alternative monetary arrangements. The Treasury could begin issuing currency competing with Federal Reserve notes, with the eventual goal of complete substitution. Parallel banking systems could develop under state charters or through private initiative, providing alternative pathways for payment and settlement. Over a transition period of perhaps a decade, the monetary base could be shifted from Fed liabilities to Treasury liabilities, with the Fed's open market operations gradually wound down.

For those attracted to the competing currencies model, complete privatization of money issuance offers an even more radical alternative. No government would define a legal tender or official currency; instead, banks and other institutions would issue their own notes denominated in various commodities or baskets of goods. Individuals and businesses would freely choose which currencies to accept, with market discipline ensuring that reliable currencies drive out unreliable ones. This system has historical precedent and theoretical justification, though it would require significant legal reform to eliminate legal tender laws and other government monopolies on money.

Addressing Objections: Why Critics Are Wrong

Those defending the current system raise several objections that deserve direct engagement. First, critics argue that a gold standard would limit the money supply excessively, causing deflation and economic stagnation. However, historical experience under the gold standard does not support this claim. The remarkable economic growth of the nineteenth century occurred with a rapidly expanding gold supply driven by new discoveries and mining technology, demonstrating that the constraint on money creation is not binding in practice. Moreover, steady or mildly falling prices, rather than being harmful, reward savers and producers, encouraging capital accumulation and long-term investment. The alleged evils of deflation are largely a creation of the fiat currency era, when economies have become dependent on continuous monetary expansion.

Second, defenders of the Fed argue that central banking is necessary to respond to financial crises and prevent bank runs. This argument, while possessing surface plausibility, fails upon closer examination. The Federal Reserve was explicitly created to prevent bank runs, yet some of the most severe banking crises in American history—including the Panic of 1907 that motivated the Fed's creation—occurred under the preceding national banking system. More importantly, the moral hazard created by the Fed's lender-of-last-resort function encourages excessive risk-taking by banks, knowing that failure will be rescued rather than allowed to bankrupt shareholders and bondholders. A free banking system with clear rules and without government guarantees would feature stronger market discipline, with banks maintaining higher reserves and taking fewer risks.

Third, some economists argue that the complexity of modern economies requires sophisticated monetary management that only a central bank can provide. This argument elevates the expertise of central planners above the distributed knowledge of millions of market participants. In reality, no group of economists, however brilliant, can possess sufficient information to set interest rates optimally for an economy of hundreds of millions of people. The market process, wherein prices adjust based on the actions of countless individuals pursuing their own interests, generates coordination far superior to any central plan. Allowing interest rates to reflect genuine time preference rather than central bank decree would improve economic calculation and allocation.

Conclusion: The Path to Monetary Liberation

Understanding the Critique of Central Banking

The critique begins with a basic observation about the nature of money and its creation. When a central bank expands the money supply, whether through quantitative easing, lowering interest rates, or simply creating new reserves, it does not create equivalent new goods and services to accompany that money. This dilution of the existing money supply, advocates argue, amounts to a hidden tax that silently erodes the purchasing power of everyone who holds currency. The Federal Reserve as an Unaccountable Institution

Critics of the Federal Reserve focus particular attention on its structural characteristics, which they view as fundamentally undemocratic and contrary to American principles. The Fed operates as an independent central bank, meaning it is largely insulated from direct political control and operates with minimal public accountability. Its board members serve long terms that cross presidential administrations, and its meetings are conducted with secrecy that extends to which specific banks received emergency lending during crises. This combination of enormous power over the economy and minimal oversight troubles those who see it as a fourth branch of government unconstrained by constitutional limitations.

The Federal Reserve's dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices is viewed skeptically by its critics, who argue that these goals are inherently contradictory and that the Fed consistently prioritizes the appearance of prosperity through monetary expansion over genuine price stability. When forced to choose between tightening monetary policy to combat inflation and loosening it to stimulate employment, the argument goes, the Fed invariably chooses expansion because the political costs of recession are immediate while the costs of inflation are delayed and diffuse. This systematic bias toward monetary expansion, critics contend, ensures that the purchasing power of the dollar will inevitably erode over time, punishing savers and those on fixed incomes while rewarding debtors and those with access to speculative capital.

The Inflation Tax and Its Distributional Effects

The central argument against fiat currency and central banking revolves around the concept of seigniorage—the profit made by issuing currency—and how its benefits and costs are distributed across society. When a central bank creates new money, the first recipients of that money benefit from it before prices have risen to reflect the increased supply. These initial recipients are typically banks, financial institutions, government agencies, and large corporations with close ties to the monetary authority. By the time the new money reaches ordinary workers in the form of wages, prices have already risen, meaning that workers effectively receive a smaller share of national income while the early recipients of new money have extracted wealth from the economy.

This process is characterized by some critics as a form of theft or fraud, albeit one conducted through legal channels and masked by economic jargon. Every holder of dollars, from the wealthy investor with millions in the bank to the minimum-wage worker with a few dollars in their pocket, sees their savings diluted by the expansion of the money supply. The inflation tax is particularly harsh on the elderly and others who have prudently saved for retirement, as the purchasing power of their nest eggs diminishes over time. Meanwhile, those who have borrowed heavily benefit, as they repay their debts with money that is worth less than when they borrowed it. Critics argue that this creates perverse incentives that discourage saving and encourage speculative borrowing and living beyond one's means.

The Business Cycle and Monetary Intervention

Austrian school economists and other critics of central banking argue that the Federal Reserve does not merely cause inflation but is fundamentally responsible for the boom-and-bust cycle that has characterized the modern economy. According to this view, when the central bank artificially lowers interest rates below the natural rate determined by time preference and the availability of real savings, it sends false signals to entrepreneurs that more capital is available for investment than actually exists. Businesses respond to these signals by undertaking ambitious projects, investing in equipment, hiring workers, and expanding capacity based on the assumption that consumer demand will match their production plans.

Eventually, the malinvestments become apparent as resources prove insufficient to complete all the projects that were begun during the boom. Projects that seemed profitable when interest rates were artificially low prove unviable at higher rates or when the money supply is eventually tightened. The bust phase then ensues as these malinvestments are liquidated, businesses fail, workers are laid off, and the economy contracts. From this perspective, the Fed does not prevent economic crises—it creates them by distorting the price signals that allow markets to coordinate production and consumption efficiently. The bust is not a failure of markets but a necessary correction following the artificial boom that central bank intervention made possible.

The Case for the Gold Standard

Advocates of returning to a gold standard argue that gold possesses unique properties that make it ideal as money. Its supply increases slowly and predictably as new gold is mined, and this increase roughly tracks the growth of the real economy over long periods. Unlike paper money, which can be created in unlimited quantities by those with the power to do so, gold cannot be counterfeited or inflated away. The discipline imposed by a gold standard forces governments to live within their means because they cannot simply print money to pay their debts or fund their programs. This constraint, critics argue, would produce more responsible fiscal policy, prevent wars and military adventurism funded by inflationary finance, and protect citizens from the erosion of their savings.

The historical record of the gold standard is contested, with proponents pointing to the relative price stability and economic growth of the classical gold standard era from roughly 1870 to 1914, and critics noting that the system was prone to deflation during periods of rapid economic growth and that it limited the ability of central banks to respond to financial crises. Supporters counter that the occasional deflation under the gold standard was mild compared to the inflation that has characterized the fiat era, and that financial crises were less severe and frequent when banks operated under the discipline of convertible currency. The gold standard, in this view, constrained the worst impulses of governments and central banks, forcing them to maintain fiscal and monetary discipline that they have proven unable to maintain when freed from such constraints.

Free Banking and Market Competition in Currency

Some critics of central banking go beyond advocating a return to the gold standard and argue for complete deregulation of monetary issuance. Under a system of free banking, any bank or private institution could issue its own currency, and the market would determine which currencies gain acceptance. Competition among issuers would, according to this view, produce stable and reliable currencies because banks that issued money that lost value through excessive expansion would lose customers to more prudent competitors. The market would impose the discipline that central bankers have proven unable or unwilling to impose on themselves.

Proponents of free banking point to historical examples such as the Scottish banking system before 1844, where multiple banks issued their own notes and competition maintained stability without a central bank. They argue that the combination of freedom of contract, the right to issue currency, and the legal framework that held banks accountable for their notes produced a remarkably stable monetary system. Under free banking, currencies would be denominated in terms of weight of precious metal or could even be designed to maintain stable purchasing power in terms of a basket of goods, giving consumers the benefit of monetary stability without the political manipulation inherent in government-issued currency.

Political and Philosophical Dimensions

The argument against central banking is not merely economic but carries significant political and philosophical dimensions. Critics see the concentration of monetary power in the hands of an unelected technocratic elite as fundamentally inconsistent with democratic governance. The Federal Reserve, they argue, has the power to determine the economic conditions under which all Americans live—their employment prospects, their wages, their ability to save for the future—yet its decisions are made by individuals who are neither elected nor subject to removal by popular vote. This represents a transfer of democratic accountability to an institution that operates in secret and answers to no one.

From this perspective, the ability to create money is ultimately the ability to tax without representation, and the Federal Reserve represents a subtle but profound shift in the nature of American governance. The founders, critics note, gave Congress the power to coin money and regulate the value thereof, a power that was meant to remain with the people's representatives and subject to democratic accountability. The creation of the Federal Reserve in 1913 and the subsequent evolution of monetary policy have transferred this power to a private corporation with public purposes, operating in a twilight zone between government and private interests. Returning the power to create money to its constitutional locus, whether through a gold standard, free banking, or some other arrangement that limits the state's capacity to inflate, is seen as essential to restoring genuine self-governance.

Conclusion: Competing Visions of Monetary Order

The arguments for abolishing the Federal Reserve, ending fiat currency, and adopting either a gold standard or free banking system represent a coherent critique of modern monetary arrangements from a particular ideological perspective. Whether one finds these arguments persuasive depends largely on prior beliefs about the proper role of government in the economy, the causes of business cycles, and the relationship between monetary policy and social welfare. Critics of central banking view their proposals as a return to sound money and limited government, while supporters of the current system argue that the flexibility provided by fiat currency allows for economic stabilization that would be impossible under more rigid monetary regimes.

What is clear is that the debate over monetary policy touches fundamental questions about economic organization, political power, and the relationship between citizens and their government. Understanding the arguments from the perspective of those who believe central banking is inflationary and harmful is essential for anyone seeking to engage seriously with these questions, regardless of which side of the debate they ultimately find most compelling.

A Speech on Restoring Economic Freedom Through the Abolition of the Federal Reserve

The Architecture of Control

To understand why we must abolish the Federal Reserve, we must first understand what the Federal Reserve actually is and what it has done to our economic fabric. When Congress created the Federal Reserve in 1913, it did so under the promise of providing economic stability, of smoothing out the business cycle, of preventing the financial panics that had periodically gripped the American economy. The architects of this system sold it as a public service, a necessary institution to safeguard the economic welfare of the American people.

What was created, instead, was an unaccountable engine of inflation, a machine that has systematically destroyed the purchasing power of every dollar earned by American workers. It is a consortium of private banking interests, operating with extraordinary power, answerable to no electorate, subject to no meaningful checks, and driven by an ideology that treats the expansion of credit as an unqualified good—regardless of the consequences for the value of money itself.

Consider what this institution has done over the course of its existence. Since the creation of the Federal Reserve, the dollar has lost approximately ninety-seven percent of its purchasing power. Ninety-seven percent. This is not a figure of political rhetoric—it is an arithmetic reality that every American family feels in their pocketbooks, in their grocery bills, in the ever-escalating cost of housing, healthcare, and education. The fundamental problem with our monetary system is not merely the Federal Reserve as an institution—it is the fiat currency system itself, the arrangement that allows an unelected board of central bankers to expand the money supply at will, creating money out of thin air and distributing it through the financial system in ways that benefit the connected few while impoverishing the working many.

Fiat currency is, at its core, an invitation to moral hazard. When money is no longer tethered to any real asset, when it is not backed by gold or silver or any scarce commodity that imposes discipline on its creation, there is no limit to how much can be printed. The temptation to print becomes irresistible, particularly for governments that find it far easier to create money to fund their spending than to tax citizens or trim their budgets. The consequences of this arrangement are visible everywhere we look. We have created an economy addicted to easy money, where asset prices are inflated by monetary manipulation rather than genuine productivity gains, where the gap between those with access to newly-created credit and those without it widens with every quantitative easing program, where speculation is rewarded and savings is punished. The inflation that the Federal Reserve creates is not neutral. It falls heaviest on those least able to protect themselves—the working class and the poor, those whose wages cannot keep pace with rising prices, whose savings are depleted, who cannot afford to hold assets that might appreciate in step with monetary expansion. Meanwhile, the wealthy, already positioned in financial assets that benefit from inflation, grow richer still. The Federal Reserve has become the greatest engine of inequality in American society, hidden behind technical jargon about "monetary policy" and "inflation targeting," but understood clearly by those who benefit from its operations.

The central conceit of the Federal Reserve system is that a small group of intelligent, well-intentioned experts can manage the money supply better than the free market can. This is the premise of central planning applied to money, and like all central planning, it has failed. The Fed's track record is not merely imperfect—it is a catalogue of catastrophic misjudgments that have brought devastating harm to millions of ordinary Americans.

Those who make the decisions about how much money to create, what interest rates to set, when to expand or contract credit, do not bear the costs of their errors. The costs are borne by the rest of us—in lost savings, in fewer opportunities, in the anxiety of economic insecurity. The alternative to our current monetary disorder is not merely the absence of the Federal Reserve—it is the establishment of a monetary system grounded in sound principles, one that imposes discipline on government, protects the value of savings, and links money to something real rather than to the whims of central planners.

A gold standard offers precisely this discipline. Under a gold standard, money is not an instrument of government policy but a commodity with intrinsic value, one that cannot be created at will by those in power. The supply of gold is determined by geological scarcity and the labor required to extract it from the earth, not by the decisions of central bankers. This imposes a hard budget constraint on government spending: if you cannot print money to fund your operations, you must either tax citizens or borrow from those who have saved. This constraint is not a flaw—it is the feature that makes sound money possible.

The historical evidence supports this conclusion. The classical gold standard era, spanning from roughly 1870 to 1914, was characterized by remarkable price stability, robust economic growth, and unprecedented expansion of living standards for ordinary people. Prices might fluctuate based on the supply of gold and the growth of the economy, but over the long run, they remained remarkably stable. Workers could plan for the future with confidence that the money they earned today would retain its value tomorrow. Savers could accumulate wealth without fearing that their efforts would be erased by monetary manipulation.

Critics will argue that a gold standard constrains economic growth, that it is too inflexible for modern economies, that it hands control over monetary policy to gold miners in South Africa or wherever gold is extracted. These criticisms deserve serious engagement, and they fail upon examination. The gold standard did not prevent the remarkable economic growth of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries—it provided the monetary foundation for that growth by ensuring stability and preventing the boom-and-bust cycles that characterize fiat currency systems. As for the critique about gold miners, this misunderstands how a gold standard actually operates: the supply of gold grows roughly in line with population and productivity over time, providing a stable monetary base without requiring active management by any central authority.

The Case for Ending the Federal Reserve and Returning to Sound Money

In 1913, the United States embarked on a monetary experiment that fundamentally transformed our economy and gradually eroded our financial sovereignty. The establishment of the Federal Reserve System represented a significant departure from the monetary principles that had guided America through its most prosperous periods of growth.
